quality_flags: The document refers to the Diabetic Retinopathy PPP in its statement about intended users, despite addressing epiretinal membrane and vitreomacular traction.
metadata.summary: This guideline addresses the presentation, diagnosis, natural history, and management of epiretinal membrane and vitreomacular traction, with additional discussion of vitreomacular adhesion. It covers observation, intravitreal gas injection, vitrectomy, surgical counseling, and postoperative follow-up. Its stated aims include preserving visual function, reducing symptoms, and supporting treatment decisions with patients.

target_population: Predominantly adults with ERM, VMT, or VMA
therapeutic_areas: Removal of the Internal Limiting Membrane

toxicities.incidence: The majority of phakic patients develop progressive nuclear cataract after vitrectomy for ERM; the rate of progression varies and may depend on age.
recognition: Development of a progressive nuclear cataract

management.actions: Cataract surgery may be postponed, recommended before vitrectomy, or performed during the same operation.

toxicities.incidence: Retinal breaks occurred in approximately 1% of cases (8 of 548) in a study of vitrectomies using a 23-gauge cannula system. A randomized trial of PVL reported higher than expected rates of retinal tear and retinal detachment, prompting early termination; it did not establish a definitive safety estimate.
recognition: A retinal break identified during examination of the retina
prevention: During vitrectomy, shave the peripheral vitreous, particularly around the cannulas, to reduce iatrogenic breaks during instrument exchanges.
After removing the tractional tissue, examine the retina for breaks or detachment.

toxicities.incidence: One study reported retinal detachment in 1% (2 of 166) of consecutive 23-gauge vitrectomies. Another reported detachment in 1% of eyes undergoing 23-gauge vitrectomy and 3.5% of eyes undergoing 20-gauge vitrectomy, among 349 eyes. A randomized PVL trial found higher than expected rates of retinal detachment and retinal tear and ended early; its small sample and early termination precluded definitive safety findings.

management.actions: Arrange an earlier or more frequent follow-up examination. Instruct patients to notify their ophthalmologist promptly about new floaters, visual-field loss, metamorphopsia, or reduced visual acuity.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Shave the peripheral vitreous, especially near the cannulas, to reduce iatrogenic retinal breaks during instrument exchanges.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients undergoing surgical removal of ERM or VMT

prophylaxis.recommendation: Avoid excessive intraoperative light exposure of the macula.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients undergoing ERM or VMT surgery

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with an ERM that is stable or causes few symptoms.
decision_rules: Most ERMs remain relatively stable and need no treatment; observation is appropriate when visual symptoms do not warrant elective surgery.
Explain that visual acuity may deteriorate over time and rarely improves on its own. Reconsider surgery if symptoms worsen or visual acuity declines.
Encourage periodic monocular assessment of central vision, including regular Amsler grid testing, to identify increasing metamorphopsia or a new small central scotoma.

recommended_regimens.name: Observation without Treatment
recommended_regimens.summary: Monitor the condition and educate the patient about progression and the availability of surgery if visual function worsens.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In a population-based study of 3654 people assessed by fundus photography over 5 years, 29% of ERMs progressed, 26% regressed, and 39% remained approximately the same; 20% of eyes with cellophane maculopathy progressed. A study of 47 eyes found no change in visual acuity or clinical appearance over a mean of 38 months. The guideline states that postponing surgery until symptoms arise does not produce a worse outcome than immediate surgery.

response_assessment.method: Monocular central-vision assessment and Amsler grid testing
response_assessment.interpretation: Increasing distortion or a newly developed small central scotoma may indicate progression.

supportive_care: Advise patients to contact their ophthalmologist promptly for increased floaters, visual-field loss, metamorphopsia, or reduced visual acuity.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: When deciding between continued observation and surgery, consider how much the patient's vision interferes with daily activities and the patient's understanding of surgical risks.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with VMT involving an area of 1500 µm or less, particularly when visual acuity remains stable.
decision_rules: Observation is an option because traction in an area of 1500 µm or less can release spontaneously.
Consider the presence of cystoid spaces when discussing prognosis: a cited study suggested a more guarded outlook for eyes with cystoid spaces at baseline.
Reconsider intervention if symptoms or visual function become sufficiently troublesome.

recommended_regimens.name: Observation without Treatment
recommended_regimens.summary: Follow visual function and symptoms while allowing time for possible spontaneous release of traction.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Across cited studies, spontaneous release from the macula occurred in 23% to 47% of eyes with VMT of 1500 µm or less during 1 to 2 years of follow-up. Release usually improved visual acuity and symptoms if it did not create a full-thickness macular hole. An earlier study found a decline of 2 Snellen lines or more in 34 of 53 eyes (64%) over 60 months; 43/53 (81%) of those eyes had cystoid macular spaces at baseline.

response_assessment.method: Assess visual acuity and symptoms; use OCT to characterize traction and associated retinal changes.
response_assessment.interpretation: Spontaneous release may lessen symptoms and improve acuity, provided a full-thickness macular hole does not develop.

supportive_care: Advise prompt contact with an ophthalmologist if metamorphopsia or visual acuity worsens.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: An area of VMT that is broad (>1500 µm), an accompanying pathologic macular detachment, or poor presenting visual acuity makes improvement without vitrectomy unlikely according to the guideline.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients troubled or functionally impaired by reduced visual acuity, metamorphopsia, diplopia, or difficulty using both eyes together.
decision_rules: Base the elective decision to operate chiefly on symptom severity, effects on activities such as reading and driving, the patient's preferences, and an informed discussion of risks and benefits.
Earlier surgery may yield better long-term visual acuity recovery than delayed surgery, but the relevant delay is measured in months rather than days.
If ERM and VMT coexist, release both sources of macular traction during surgery.

recommended_regimens.name: Vitrectomy surgery
recommended_regimens.summary: Elective vitrectomy with removal of the ERM when its visual effects warrant intervention. The cited Cochrane review found no randomized controlled trial comparing surgery with no intervention; its associated ratings are I- and Insufficient quality.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The guideline reports that, on average, approximately 80% of patients with ERM or VMT improve by at least 2 lines of visual acuity after vitrectomy. It also reports that 10% to 20% of patients have unchanged or worse vision following surgery. Metamorphopsia usually improves and may resolve, although visual results vary.

alternative_regimens.name: ERM and ILM removal
alternative_regimens.summary: ILM peeling may be added to ERM removal. A systematic review of 13 studies found similar visual acuity between groups but greater anatomical success with ILM peeling; its associated ratings are I+, Good quality, Discretionary recommendation. A separate 2021 systematic review found similar visual acuity but less recurrence with ILM peeling at 6 to 12 months postoperatively; its associated ratings are I-, Moderate quality, Discretionary recommendation.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider alongside ERM removal without ILM peeling after discussing potentially lower recurrence and the uncertain functional effect of possible inner retinal tissue loss. Other cited studies found no difference in recurrence or found faster retinal-sensitivity recovery without ILM peeling.

response_assessment.timepoint: Postoperative day 1 and again 1 to 2 weeks following surgery, or sooner if symptoms or early findings warrant
response_assessment.method: Obtain an interval symptom history; measure intraocular pressure; examine the anterior segment, wound sites, and central retina by slit lamp when possible; and examine the peripheral retina with indirect binocular ophthalmoscopy.
response_assessment.interpretation: High or low intraocular pressure, wound leakage, pain, worsening vision, or concern for a retinal complication warrants earlier or more frequent review.

supportive_care: Before surgery, discuss potential cataract, retinal tears or detachment, endophthalmitis, retinal damage with vision loss, ERM recurrence, and postoperative intraocular-pressure changes.
Counsel about postoperative medications, retinal-detachment symptoms, and precautions if intraocular gas was used.
Consider referral to a strabismus specialist or orthoptist for persistent diplopia or difficulty using both eyes together.
Refer patients with functionally limiting postoperative visual impairment for vision rehabilitation and social services.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Cataract progression after pars plana vitrectomy is common in phakic eyes. If cataract is already present, its surgery may be deferred, performed before vitrectomy, or combined with it. A cited systematic review and meta-analysis found no significant difference in complications or visual and refractive outcomes between combined and sequential pars plana vitrectomy and phacoemulsification for macular hole or epiretinal membrane. Visual acuity and distortion may improve without resolving completely, and acuity can sometimes decline without recovery. Minimize excessive intraoperative macular light exposure.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients whose VMT-related visual impairment or symptoms justify elective intervention, particularly those with broad VMT (>1500 µm), accompanying pathologic macular detachment, or poor presenting visual acuity.
decision_rules: Discuss observation versus surgery in light of interference with daily activities, symptom severity, the patient's preferences, and the risks and benefits.
The guideline states that VMT with broad attachment (>1500 µm), pathologic macular detachment, or poor initial visual acuity does not typically improve without vitrectomy.
Remove any coexisting ERM as well as the VMT to relieve macular traction.

recommended_regimens.name: Vitrectomy surgery
recommended_regimens.summary: Elective surgical release of VMT when its impact on vision warrants intervention. The cited Cochrane review found no randomized controlled trial comparing surgery with no intervention; its associated ratings are I- and Insufficient quality.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The guideline reports that, on average, approximately 80% of patients with ERM or VMT improve by at least 2 lines of visual acuity after vitrectomy, while 10% to 20% have unchanged or worse vision. In a cited meta-analysis of 259 eyes from 17 articles with VMT, mean preoperative logMAR was 0.67 and mean postoperative logMAR was 0.42; 33% gained 2 or more lines, and 21% had unchanged or reduced postoperative visual acuity.

response_assessment.timepoint: Postoperative day 1 and again 1 to 2 weeks following surgery, or earlier as indicated
response_assessment.method: Review symptoms, measure intraocular pressure, inspect the anterior segment and wounds, examine the central retina when possible, and perform indirect binocular examination of the peripheral retina.
response_assessment.interpretation: Arrange earlier or more frequent assessment for abnormal intraocular pressure, wound leakage, pain, declining vision, or a suspected retinal complication.

supportive_care: Discuss surgical risks and potential benefits before obtaining informed consent.
Provide instructions on postoperative medicines, retinal-detachment warning symptoms, and intraocular-gas precautions when applicable.
Consider referral for persistent diplopia or difficulty coordinating the eyes after surgery.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Surgery is elective rather than urgent. When a full-thickness or deep lamellar hole is suspected during surgery, the guideline describes a more complete fluid-gas exchange using a nonexpansile or minimally expansile concentration of C3F8 or SF6 gas. Visual improvement is not assured.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients being considered for intravitreal gas injection to release VMT.
decision_rules: The guideline presents intravitreal gas as an investigated means of releasing VMT, but does not establish it as a preferred treatment.
Because trial findings do not provide clear guidance, clinicians need to exercise judgment and counsel patients closely about risks and benefits using the limited available evidence.

alternative_regimens.name: Gas Injection for Vitreomacular Traction
alternative_regimens.summary: Small cited cohorts reported VMT release after intravitreal gas. A DRCR Retina Network randomized trial of pneumatic vitreolysis using intravitreal C3F8 gas versus sham injection ended early because retinal detachment and tear rates in the gas group were higher than expected; its small sample and early termination prevented definitive safety and efficacy findings.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The guideline does not specify eligibility criteria or a preferred place in treatment. Discuss the uncertain evidence and retinal risks with the patient.

response_assessment.method: Assess whether VMT has released from the macula.
response_assessment.interpretation: The small cited studies measured release within 1 month; the guideline does not establish a response threshold for clinical decisions.

supportive_care: Counsel closely about potential retinal detachment and retinal tear.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Reported VMT release within 1 month was 40% in a cohort of 15 eyes, 73% in a cohort of 30 eyes, and 56% in a study of 9 eyes using SF6 gas. Another study of 56 eyes using 0.3 ml pure C3F8 reported VMT release of 85.7% and closure of small holes of 60%. In the DRCR Retina Network randomized trial, central-macular VMT release occurred in 78% of eyes in the pneumatic vitreolysis group versus 9% in the sham-injection group; the trial stopped early for safety concerns.

conditions.name: Epiretinal membrane
conditions.description: A fibrocellular sheet on the inner surface of the neurosensory retina. It may leave the underlying retina apparently normal or contract and distort the macula, retinal vessels and foveal contour. Idiopathic ERM has no clearly identifiable cause; secondary ERM can follow retinal disease, injury or ocular procedures.
conditions.epidemiology: ERM becomes more common with age and is estimated to affect approximately 30 million U.S. adults aged 43 to 86 years. It is bilateral in up to 20% to 35% of cases. Population-study prevalence ranges from 2.2% and 3.4% in the Beijing Eye Study and rural Handan Eye Study, respectively, to 7% and 8.9% in two Australian populations and 18.8% and 28.9% among Los Angeles Latino individuals and participants in MESA. SD-OCT found a prevalence of 34.1% at the 20-year Beaver Dam Eye Study follow-up, whose participants had a mean age of 74.1 years. Among eyes without clinically evident macular pathology before cataract surgery, routine SD-OCT detected ERM in 2.2% to 11.0%. Increasing age is a consistent risk factor. A 2016 systematic review including over 49,000 subjects found significantly higher risk only with greater age and female gender, although the guideline describes female gender among other proposed risk factors that have not been confirmed consistently.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Vision may remain stable with few symptoms or deteriorate progressively. Patients may report reduced visual acuity, metamorphopsia, diplopia, difficulty using both eyes together, or problems reading and driving; some close the affected eye while reading. Examination may show a thin, translucent membrane or a thicker, white fibrotic membrane, which is more likely to cause symptoms and macular displacement. Contraction may produce retinal folds, vascular traction, foveal distortion, cystoid spaces or a macular hole.

subtypes.name: Idiopathic ERM
subtypes.distinguishing_features: No cause can be clearly identified.

subtypes.name: Secondary ERM
subtypes.distinguishing_features: May occur after retinal breaks or detachment, intraocular surgery, trauma, retinal laser treatment or cryotherapy; it also occurs with retinal vascular disease or inflammation.

subtypes.name: cellophane maculopathy
subtypes.distinguishing_features: An early, generally asymptomatic form with a thin, translucent appearance. Reported prevalence ranges from 1.8% and 2.2% in urban and rural China to 16.3% among Los Angeles Latino individuals and 25.1% in MESA.

subtypes.name: preretinal macular fibrosis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A thicker or more opaque form associated with symptomatic ERM. Reported prevalence ranges from 0.7% in rural China to 3.5% among Asian Indian individuals, 3.8% in MESA and 3.9% in Melbourne, Australia.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Examine the membrane and its effects on the macula.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A membrane may be thin and translucent or thicker and fibrotic; associated findings can include retinal folds, altered vessels and a distorted or absent foveal depression.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Exclude an optic pit or advanced cupping.

Assess central visual distortion and help monitor change.

diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A change in central vision may indicate increasing metamorphopsia or a developing central scotoma.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Clinically assess a suspected full thickness macular hole.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When a full thickness macular hole is suspected.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Diagnose and characterize ERM and associated retinal changes.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Routinely during diagnostic evaluation; also useful for comparison with a normal eye when explaining findings to a patient.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: ERM typically forms a hyper-reflective, sometimes irregular layer on the inner retinal surface. Findings may include points of attachment separated by hyporeflective spaces, elevation of the foveal depression, retinal folds, macular thickening and cystoid spaces. Images can also demonstrate a lamellar macular hole or concurrent VMT.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate ERM and detect associated retinal vascular, neovascular or inflammatory pathology.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When ancillary evaluation of ERM or possible associated retinal disease may be helpful.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An early ERM may have a relatively normal angiogram. With contraction, macular vessels may become tortuous or straightened around the traction site; leakage, dye pooling in cystoid spaces, capillary dropout, telangiectasia, collateral vessels or microaneurysms may provide further diagnostic information.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Help evaluate ERM and identify associated retinal pathology.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When ancillary evaluation may be helpful.

follow_up.schedule: During observation, patients should monitor central vision periodically in each eye and report changes promptly; no fixed observation interval is specified. After surgery, examination is advised on postoperative day 1 and again 1 to 2 weeks later, or sooner if symptoms or early findings warrant it.
recommended_tests: Regular monocular Amsler grid testing during observation.
Postoperative interval history, including new symptoms.
Postoperative slit-lamp biomicroscopy of the anterior segment, wound sites and central retina when possible.
Postoperative indirect binocular ophthalmoscopy of the peripheral retina.
long_term_effects: Visual acuity may worsen over time, while spontaneous improvement is rare.
Following vitrectomy, most phakic patients develop progressive nuclear cataract.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Patients should promptly report more floaters, visual-field loss, increasing metamorphopsia or reduced visual acuity. Earlier or more frequent postoperative assessment may be needed for abnormal intraocular pressure, wound leakage, pain, worsening vision or concern about a retinal complication. Persistent functionally limiting visual impairment warrants referral for vision rehabilitation and social services.

conditions.name: Vitreomacular traction
conditions.description: VMT develops when the posterior cortical vitreous separates from the surrounding retina but remains attached near the macular center, exerting traction that changes macular anatomy. Possible consequences include thickening, distortion, intraretinal cystoid spaces, subretinal fluid or tractional macular detachment. It may coexist with ERM.
conditions.epidemiology: VMT is less common than ERM and is estimated to affect 0.4% to 2.0% of U.S. adults over the age of 63. Its prevalence rises with age. Among 13/20 eyes (65%) with VMT in one cited study, ERM was also present.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Patients may have reduced visual acuity, metamorphopsia, diplopia or difficulty using both eyes together. Symptoms may be acute or chronic, depending on traction severity and the resulting macular distortion or detachment. Visual acuity often changes little over short-term follow-up.

subtypes.name: localized vitreomacular attachment
subtypes.distinguishing_features: An attachment of about 500 µm can elevate and pull on the fovea, with subsequent intraretinal cystoid spaces.

subtypes.name: broad attachment
subtypes.distinguishing_features: An attachment of about 1500 µm (approximately 1 disc diameter) can produce greater macular elevation, potentially reaching retinal detachment, but is less likely to have intraretinal cystoid spaces.

diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The posterior hyaloid remains attached to part of the macula while separating in the surrounding region. Traction can be focal or extend across the macula; cystoid spaces and concurrent ERM may be visible.

follow_up.schedule: No fixed schedule is stated for observation. After surgery, examination is advised on postoperative day 1 and again 1 to 2 weeks later, with earlier review when new symptoms or findings arise.
recommended_tests: Postoperative interval history, including new symptoms.
Postoperative slit-lamp biomicroscopy of the anterior segment, wound sites and central retina when possible.
Postoperative indirect binocular ophthalmoscopy of the peripheral retina.

An earlier cited study reported a decline of 2 Snellen lines or more in 34 of 53 eyes (64%) over 60 months; 43/53 (81%) had cystoid macular spaces at baseline, which may indicate a more guarded prognosis.
Patients with broad VMT (>1500 µm), accompanying pathologic macular detachment, or poor presenting visual acuity do not typically improve without vitrectomy.
Following vitrectomy, most phakic patients develop progressive nuclear cataract.

Patients should promptly report increased floaters, visual-field loss, metamorphopsia or reduced visual acuity.

conditions.name: Vitreomacular adhesion
conditions.description: Attachment of the posterior cortical vitreous to the macula without resulting traction. It may be part of the usual progression toward posterior vitreous detachment.
conditions.clinical_presentation: VMA is often asymptomatic. Unlike VMT, the attachment does not produce secondary retinal pathology.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Examine the vitreoretinal interface.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Exclude an optic pit or advanced cupping.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess for retinal breaks or other pathology.
Assess central vision.

diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A foveal attachment persists despite separation of the posterior vitreous face elsewhere, without secondary retinal changes caused by the attachment.

therapies_index.name: Observation without Treatment
approved_indications: ERM with stable vision and few symptoms
VMT when observation is chosen after considering symptoms, visual function, and the risks of intervention
therapies_index.administration: Patients are advised to check central vision periodically in each eye separately, including regular monocular Amsler grid testing, and to report signs of progression.
monitoring: Changes in visual acuity, metamorphopsia, or a central scotoma
New or worsening symptoms, including increased floaters or visual-field loss

therapies_index.name: Vitrectomy surgery
therapies_index.mechanism: Surgical removal of vitreous attachments and ERM releases traction on the macula.
approved_indications: ERM or VMT causing bothersome loss of visual acuity, metamorphopsia, double vision, or difficulty using both eyes together
therapies_index.administration: Usually an elective procedure. Surgery commonly uses a 23-, 25-, or a 27-gauge vitrectomy system with local, monitored anesthesia care. When VMT and ERM coexist, both tractional elements are removed from the retinal surface.
key_toxicities: Progressive nuclear cataract develops in the majority of phakic patients after vitrectomy for ERM.
Retinal breaks, retinal detachment, endophthalmitis, macular hole formation, and vision loss from retinal damage are possible.
Postoperative intraocular pressure may rise or fall, particularly in patients with glaucoma.
Vision may remain unchanged or worsen; overall, 10% to 20% of patients have unchanged or worse vision after surgery.
monitoring: Examination on postoperative day 1 and again 1 to 2 weeks after surgery, or earlier if symptoms or examination findings warrant it
Anterior segment, wound sites, central retina when possible, and peripheral retina
Pain, wound leakage, worsening vision, and signs of retinal complications

therapies_index.name: ERM removal
therapies_index.mechanism: Peeling the membrane removes a source of macular traction.
approved_indications: Surgical management of symptomatic ERM, including when ERM accompanies VMT
therapies_index.administration: The membrane is elevated and peeled with intraocular instruments during vitrectomy; the ILM may also be removed.

therapies_index.name: ILM peeling
therapies_index.mechanism: Removal of the ILM may release residual macular traction more completely; studies cited in the guideline report mixed findings on recurrence.
approved_indications: An optional component of surgery for ERM
therapies_index.administration: The ILM is peeled during vitrectomy, often after ERM removal and sometimes with a visualization agent.
key_toxicities: Loss of inner retinal tissue has been associated with ILM peeling, although its functional effect is unclear.
In a cited study, active ILM peeling delayed visual recovery compared with no peeling.
monitoring: Postoperative visual recovery and ERM recurrence

therapies_index.name: pneumatic vitreolysis (PVL)
therapies_index.mechanism: An intravitreal gas injection can release vitreomacular traction.
approved_indications: Investigated as an intervention for VMT; the guideline states that limited trial evidence does not provide definitive guidance on its safety or efficacy.
therapies_index.administration: Intravitreal injection of C3F8 gas was evaluated against sham injection in a randomized trial.
key_toxicities: Higher-than-expected rates of retinal detachment and retinal tear in the PVL group led to early termination of the cited trial.
monitoring: Release of VMT from the central macula

therapies_index.name: intravitreal gas
therapies_index.mechanism: Intravitreal gas injection may induce release of VMT.
approved_indications: Reported as an intervention for VMT in the cited studies
therapies_index.administration: Injection into the vitreous cavity; the reported studies assessed release within 1 month.
monitoring: Precautions concerning intraocular gas after surgery

therapies_index.name: C3F8 gas
therapies_index.mechanism: When injected intravitreally, the gas may induce release of VMT.
approved_indications: Studied for VMT release
Used during fluid-gas exchange when a full-thickness or deep lamellar hole is suspected
therapies_index.administration: One cited VMT study used 0.3 ml pure C3F8. For fluid-gas exchange, the guideline describes a nonexpansile or minimally expansile concentration.
key_toxicities: A randomized trial of PVL using intravitreal C3F8 reported higher-than-expected rates of retinal detachment and retinal tear, prompting early termination.
monitoring: VMT release and retinal complications after PVL
Postoperative intraocular gas precautions when used in surgery

therapies_index.name: SF6 gas
therapies_index.mechanism: Intravitreal gas may induce release of VMT.
approved_indications: Used for VMT in a cited small study
Used during fluid-gas exchange when a full-thickness or deep lamellar hole is suspected
therapies_index.administration: The surgical fluid-gas exchange uses a nonexpansile or minimally expansile concentration.
monitoring: VMT release when used for traction
Postoperative intraocular gas precautions when used in surgery

therapies_index.name: fluid-gas exchange
approved_indications: Performed more completely when the surgeon suspects a full-thickness or deep lamellar hole
therapies_index.administration: Uses a nonexpansile or minimally expansile concentration of C3F8 or SF6 gas.
monitoring: Postoperative precautions related to intraocular gas

document_sections.heading: RETINA/VITREOUS PREFERRED PRACTICE PATTERN® DEVELOPMENT PROCESS AND PARTICIPANTS
document_sections.content: The Retina/Vitreous Preferred Practice Pattern Committee developed the guideline through repeated discussion and revision of drafts until it reached consensus. The Preferred Practice Patterns Committee reviewed it in June 2024. A wider review in July 2024 sought feedback on recommendation quality, feasibility, applicability, and barriers and facilitators to implementation, including perspectives from patients and other stakeholders. The guideline is scheduled for formal reassessment in 2029, with annual committee review or earlier review when developments warrant.

document_sections.heading: OBJECTIVES OF PREFERRED PRACTICE PATTERN® GUIDELINES
document_sections.content: Preferred Practice Pattern guidelines identify features of quality eye care using the best available evidence and, where necessary, committee judgment. They guide general practice rather than determine care for every individual. Following them cannot guarantee success, and reasonable approaches outside them may be appropriate. Clinicians retain responsibility for decisions tailored to each patient. References to products are illustrative, not endorsements; some uses may fall outside approved FDA labeling or be confined to research. Clinicians must determine regulatory status and obtain appropriate consent. The guidelines remain valid for 5 years after approval unless replaced sooner. The document refers to quality-care criteria in Appendix 1 and disease codes in Appendix 2. Its statement naming the intended users refers to the Diabetic Retinopathy PPP rather than this guideline.

document_sections.heading: METHODS AND KEY TO RATINGS
document_sections.content: The guideline uses approaches from SIGN and GRADE. Individual studies receive SIGN-based evidence ratings: I++ denotes high-quality meta-analyses, reviews of RCTs, or RCTs with very low bias risk; I+ denotes well-conducted versions with low bias risk; I- denotes versions with high bias risk. II++ covers high-quality reviews or studies of case-control or cohort designs with very low confounding or bias risk and high likelihood of causality. II+ covers well-conducted case-control or cohort studies with low confounding or bias risk and moderate likelihood of causality; II- covers such studies with high confounding or bias risk and substantial doubt about causality. III denotes nonanalytic studies. GRADE rates the overall evidence as Good quality when further research is very unlikely to change confidence in the effect estimate; Moderate quality when it is likely to affect confidence substantially and may change the estimate; and Insufficient quality when it is very likely to affect confidence substantially, probably change the estimate, or leave the effect highly uncertain. Strong recommendation applies when desirable effects clearly outweigh undesirable effects, or clearly do not. Discretionary recommendation applies when that balance is less certain because evidence quality is low or effects are closely balanced. Ratings for care recommendations appear in the main text. PubMed update searches took place on March 6, 2023, January 23, 2024, and August 6, 2024. The committee screened relevant systematic reviews identified by CEV@US, and its methodologist rated them. Recommendation development considered benefits, harms, risks, and their balance; decisions used informal consensus, with voting for unresolved disagreement and abstention by members with direct financial relationships in the disputed area.

document_sections.heading: HIGHLIGHTED FINDINGS AND RECOMMENDATIONS FOR CARE
document_sections.content: Increasing age and retinal disorders or events—including PVD, uveitis, retinal breaks, retinal vein occlusions, diabetic retinopathy, and ocular inflammation—are ERM risk factors. Most ERMs remain fairly stable without treatment. For VMT involving 1500 µm or less, spontaneous macular traction release occurs in approximately 30% to 40% of eyes during 1 to 2 years of follow-up. OCT is routinely used because it is highly sensitive for ERM, VMT, and accompanying retinal changes. Vitrectomy is often indicated when reduced visual acuity, metamorphopsia, double vision, or difficulty using both eyes affects the patient. It generally improves acuity and metamorphopsia; approximately 80% of patients with ERM or VMT gain at least 2 visual-acuity lines after surgery.

document_sections.heading: DISEASE DEFINITION
document_sections.content: ERMs are sheetlike formations on the inner neurosensory retinal surface. VMA is posterior cortical vitreous attachment at the macula without traction. VMT arises when posterior cortical vitreous detaches incompletely, leaving attachments that pull on the neurosensory retina. VMT can produce macular thickening, distortion, intraretinal cystoid changes, a macular hole, or subretinal fluid. ERM and VMT can each cause reduced acuity, metamorphopsia, difficulty coordinating both eyes, and diplopia.

document_sections.heading: PATIENT POPULATION
document_sections.content: The population addressed consists predominantly of adults.

document_sections.heading: CLINICAL OBJECTIVES
document_sections.content: The objectives are to explain ERM and VMT pathogenesis, recognize their signs and symptoms, describe untreated natural history, develop a treatment approach, inform patients about options, and improve visual function or relieve symptoms.

document_sections.heading: BACKGROUND
document_sections.content: ERMs consist of fibrocellular growth over the neurosensory retina and may or may not wrinkle it. They contain reactive cells, vitreous structures, and fibrotic material. Idiopathic ERM has no clearly identifiable cause. Secondary ERM may follow retinal breaks or detachment, intraocular surgery, trauma, retinal laser treatment, or cryotherapy; a reactive healing response involving retinal pigment epithelial or glial cells is considered likely. ERM also occurs with retinal vascular disease or inflammation. A 2016 systematic review including over 49,000 participants found significantly higher ERM risk only with greater age and female gender.

document_sections.heading: INCIDENCE AND PREVALENCE
document_sections.content: ERM and VMT are relatively common and become more prevalent with age; VMT is less common. Estimated VMT prevalence among U.S. adults over 63 is 0.4% to 2.0%. An estimated approximately 30 million U.S. adults aged 43 to 86 have ERM, which may be bilateral in up to 20% to 35% of cases. Reported ERM prevalence is 2.2% in the Beijing Eye Study, 3.4% in the rural Handan Eye Study, 7% and 8.9% in two Australian populations, 18.8% among Los Angeles Latino individuals, and 28.9% in MESA. Most studies assessed ERM using nonmydriatic retinal photographs. SD-OCT at the Beaver Dam Eye Study 20-year assessment, when mean participant age was 74.1 years, found 34.1% prevalence. Among eyes without clinically apparent macular disease before cataract surgery, routine SD-OCT found ERM prevalence of 2.2% to 11.0%. Early, often asymptomatic cellophane maculopathy was more frequent than thicker, symptomatic preretinal macular fibrosis in most studied populations. Cellophane maculopathy prevalence was 1.8% and 2.2% in urban and rural China, 16.3% among Los Angeles Latino individuals, and 25.1% in MESA; diabetes and hypercholesterolemia were associated with higher rates. Preretinal macular fibrosis prevalence ranged from 0.7% in rural China to 3.5% among Asian Indian individuals, 3.8% in MESA, and 3.9% in Melbourne. Differences in tests, ERM classification, and population characteristics may account for prevalence variation. OCT is regarded as the diagnostic standard; artificial intelligence applied to fundus photographs or ophthalmoscopy is being investigated because those approaches may be cheaper and more accessible.

document_sections.heading: RISK FACTORS
document_sections.content: Studies consistently identify greater age as an ERM risk factor. Reported racial and ethnic patterns vary: MESA found any ERM in 39.0% of people of Chinese ancestry, 29.3% of Hispanic participants, 27.5% of White participants, and 26.2% of Black participants, whereas studies in China reported 2.2% and 3.4%. ERM is more frequent with uveitis or other ocular inflammation, retinal breaks, retinal vein occlusions, proliferative diabetic retinopathy, and after cataract surgery. It may accompany reduced acuity or visual-field loss, particularly when more severe. Proposed but unconfirmed risk factors include female gender, myopia, hyperopia, smoking, higher education, diabetes, hypercholesterolemia, narrow retinal arterioles, higher body mass index, genetics, and stroke. A case report described VMT developing during treatment with 1% topical pilocarpine drops and resolving when they were stopped.

document_sections.heading: Epiretinal Membrane
document_sections.content: One longstanding hypothesis proposes that PVD creates small ILM breaks through which retinal glial or retinal pigment epithelial cells migrate and proliferate. Observations of retinal pigment epithelial cells, fibrous astrocytes, astrocytes, and fibrocytes in ERMs without apparent retinal breaks or prior ocular procedures supported it. Another increasingly accepted hypothesis holds that breaks are unnecessary: cortical vitreous remnants on the ILM may contain cells that become activated myofibroblasts and form a contracting membrane. ERM can occur without obvious PVD; a surgical study found posterior vitreous attachment in 20.1% of eyes with idiopathic ERM. Vitreous remnants can persist on the retina after PVD, and a Weiss ring does not establish complete separation of the posterior hyaloid from the entire posterior retina. Hyalocytes are a major cellular component of idiopathic ERM; they originate from bone-marrow-derived cells rather than being native vitreous cells and are continually renewed. Specimens also consistently contain extracellular matrix. Retinal glial cells, hyalocytes, fibroblast or myofibroblast differentiation, collagen, and extracellular matrix contribute in varying combinations, suggesting multiple possible ERM origins.

document_sections.heading: Vitreomacular Traction
document_sections.content: PVD can progress slowly, leaving macular attachments that exert traction. OCT-based descriptions distinguish smaller from larger attachment areas. A localized attachment of about 500 µm can elevate the fovea and produce intraretinal cystoid spaces. A broader attachment of about 1500 µm (approximately 1 disc diameter) can elevate the macula as far as retinal detachment, although cystoid spaces are less likely in that configuration. Attachment size spans a continuum from pinpoint to over 1500 µm; spontaneous release is more likely with focal adhesion. ERMs may form between an attached vitreous surface and the neurosensory retina; their firm ILM adherence may help anchor residual vitreous attachment and contribute to VMT.

document_sections.heading: PATIENT OUTCOME CRITERIA
document_sections.content: Desired outcomes are prevention of vision loss and functional impairment, improved visual function, fewer symptoms such as metamorphopsia and diplopia, and preserved or improved quality of life.

document_sections.heading: History
document_sections.content: Many patients with ERM have few symptoms and stable vision; others develop progressively impaired vision. Metamorphopsia or diplopia may disrupt reading, driving, or binocular use, and patients may close one eye while reading to avoid distortion. VMT can cause similar acute or chronic impairment depending on traction severity and macular distortion or detachment. Visual acuity in either condition often changes little during short-term follow-up. VMA is frequently asymptomatic.

document_sections.heading: Examination
document_sections.content: Assessment includes a comprehensive adult eye examination, emphasizing slit-lamp evaluation of the macula and vitreoretinal interface; optic-disc biomicroscopy to exclude an optic pit or advanced cupping; indirect peripheral retinal examination with scleral depression for breaks or other disease; and an Amsler grid test. For a suspected full-thickness macular hole, the Watzke-Allen sign tests whether the patient perceives an interruption in a narrow light beam directed across the suspected defect.

document_sections.heading: Diagnostic Tests
document_sections.content: OCT is routinely used and highly sensitive for VMA, ERM, VMT, and related retinal abnormalities. Comparing affected-eye scans with normal-eye scans can aid patient understanding. ERM commonly appears as a hyperreflective, sometimes irregular inner-retinal layer, with attachment points and intervening hyporeflective separations that produce a corrugated cross-section. Its traction may elevate the foveal depression, fold the inner retina, thicken the macula, and create cystoid spaces. OCT can show lamellar macular holes with varying inner-retinal tissue loss and defined edges influenced by ERM traction. With VMT, the posterior hyaloid remains attached at the macula but separates around it; cystoid spaces may affect the entire macula. VMT traction is presumed to act anteriorly and posteriorly, in contrast to the more tangential pull of ERM. VMT ranges from focal to broad macular attachment, and both disorders commonly coexist. One series found macular vitreous adherence in 57% of 60 ERM eyes; another identified ERM in 13/20 eyes (65%) with VMT. OCT through the optic nerve also helps identify vitreopapillary traction, which can resemble disc edema or, when bilateral, papilledema. A possible relationship between vitreopapillary traction and reduced vision or ischemic optic neuropathy remains a suspicion.

document_sections.heading: Ancillary Tests
document_sections.content: Fluorescein angiography or OCTA may help assess ERM or VMT and detect associated conditions, including branch retinal vein occlusion, diabetic retinopathy, macular telangiectasia, choroidal neovascularization, and inflammatory disease. Angiography may appear nearly normal with early ERM. Increasing contraction may bend vessels toward or straighten them around the traction center. Traction on capillaries can cause leakage detectable by comparing early and late images; dye can collect in cystoid spaces, particularly during recirculation. Foveal staining and leakage usually differ from the more uniformly circular, petaloid appearance of pseudophakic cystoid macular edema, which often also produces late optic-nerve hyperfluorescence. Capillary dropout, telangiectasia, collateral vessels, or microaneurysms suggest underlying retinal vascular disease. Fluorescein crosses the placenta and remains in breastmilk for 72 hours.

document_sections.heading: Nonsurgical
document_sections.content: Patients should be told that most ERMs remain fairly stable and need no therapy. Acuity can deteriorate over time and rarely improves spontaneously, but surgery is available if symptoms worsen or acuity declines. Patients should periodically check central vision one eye at a time, including with an Amsler grid, and watch for increasing metamorphopsia or a new small central scotoma.

document_sections.heading: Observation without Treatment
document_sections.content: A population study of 3654 people using fundus photographs found ERM progression in only 29% over 5 years, regression in 26%, and approximate stability in 39%; among eyes with cellophane maculopathy, only 20% progressed in that period. In a clinical series of 34 eyes with ERM and lamellar macular holes, vision remained unchanged over a mean 18 months, although two eyes developed full-thickness holes. A study of 47 ERM eyes found stable acuity and clinical appearance over a mean 38 months. An SD-OCT study found ERM separation in 16 of 1091 (1.5%) eyes with pre-existing PVD and 21/157 (13.6%) without apparent PVD over a mean 33 months; acuity improved after separation in both groups. Most ERMs remain stable after presentation, and delaying surgery until symptoms appear does not worsen outcomes compared with immediate surgery. In VMT of 1500 µm or less, acuity is often stable and spontaneous macular traction release occurs in 23% to 47% of eyes over 1 to 2 years. Release usually improves vision and symptoms if it does not produce a full-thickness hole. An earlier study found loss of 2 Snellen lines or more in 34 of 53 eyes (64%) during 60 months; 43/53 (81%) had baseline cystoid macular spaces, which may identify a group with a less favorable prognosis.

document_sections.heading: Gas Injection for Vitreomacular Traction
document_sections.content: Studies of intravitreal gas reported VMT release within 1 month in 40% of 15 eyes, 73% of 30 eyes, and 56% of 9 eyes treated with SF6. Another study of 56 eyes using 0.3 ml pure C3F8 reported 85.7% VMT release and 60% closure of small holes. In a randomized DRCR Retina Network trial, central VMT released in 78% of PVL-treated eyes after C3F8 injection versus 9% after sham injection. Unexpectedly high retinal-detachment and retinal-tear rates in the PVL group prompted early termination for safety. The small sample and early termination precluded definitive conclusions about PVL safety or efficacy. Because trials do not provide clear guidance, clinicians need to judge its potential use individually and discuss the limited evidence, risks, and benefits closely with patients.

document_sections.heading: Vitrectomy Surgery
document_sections.content: A Cochrane review found no randomized controlled trial comparing surgery with no intervention (I-, Insufficient quality). Decisions about ERM/VMT surgery generally depend on symptom severity and disruption of daily activities. Clinicians should ask specifically about visual distress, reading, driving, and distortion. Vitrectomy is elective, not urgent. Earlier ERM surgery may yield better long-term acuity than delayed surgery, but relevant delays are measured in months rather than days. Broad VMT (>1500 µm), associated pathologic macular detachment, or poor presenting acuity makes improvement without vitrectomy atypical. Choosing observation or surgery mainly depends on the patient's visual discomfort and understanding of risks; intervention requires careful consent and discussion of benefits and harms.

document_sections.heading: Preoperative Discussion for Vitrectomy
document_sections.content: Consent discussions should weigh possible visual improvement against cataract, retinal tears or detachment, endophthalmitis, and vision loss from retinal injury. Cataract progression after pars plana vitrectomy is common in phakic eyes, with rates varying and possibly depending on age. Existing cataract surgery may be deferred, performed before vitrectomy, or combined with it. Anesthesia is usually monitored local anesthesia; general anesthesia may be suitable, particularly for anxious or claustrophobic patients. Acuity, distortion, and diplopia often improve without necessarily resolving; occasionally acuity declines permanently. ERM can recur, and postoperative intraocular pressure may increase or decrease, particularly in patients with glaucoma. The surgeon should arrange postoperative care and communicate instructions.

document_sections.heading: Technique
document_sections.content: When ERM and VMT coexist, removing both sources of macular traction is necessary. Some surgeons suggest additional ILM removal to release traction more fully and reduce recurrence; a study found residual glial and fibrotic elements on the ILM retinal surface after ERM removal in 80% of specimens, offering a possible explanation. Surgery commonly uses a 23-, 25-, or a 27-gauge vitrectomy system with monitored local anesthesia. After core vitreous removal, the posterior hyaloid is detached from the optic nerve and macula, peripheral vitreous is managed to reduce instrument-related breaks, and ERM—frequently with ILM—is peeled using intraocular instruments. Indocyanine green dye, trypan blue, or triamcinolone may be used off-label for visualization; Brilliant Blue G Ophthalmic Solution (TISSUEBLUE®, Dutch Ophthalmic, US) received FDA approval in 2019 as another visualization option with safety data. Dye safety remains somewhat disputed, although very low concentrations appear safe to many surgeons and may reduce retinal trauma by making ILM easier to see. Excessive macular light exposure during surgery should be minimized. The retina is examined afterward for breaks or detachment. A small air bubble may help seal unsutured sclerotomies; suspected full-thickness or deep lamellar holes prompt more complete fluid-gas exchange with nonexpansile or minimally expansile C3F8 or SF6.

document_sections.heading: Removal of the Internal Limiting Membrane
document_sections.content: Table 1 compares ERM removal alone with combined ERM and ILM peeling. Five included studies found less ERM recurrence with ILM peeling; two found no difference. ILM peeling may remove inner-retinal tissue, but the functional consequence is uncertain. A review of 13 studies found similar visual acuity between approaches and greater anatomical success with ILM peeling (I+, Good quality, Discretionary recommendation). A separate randomized-trial meta-analysis found no significant improvement in visual outcome or ERM recurrence with ILM peeling. One study found faster and greater retinal-sensitivity recovery without ILM peeling. A 2021 review found similar visual acuity with either approach but less recurrence after ILM peeling at 6 to 12 months (I-, Moderate quality, Discretionary recommendation). The table provides individual study designs, numbers of eyes, follow-up, results, and which approach—if any—was favored.

document_sections.heading: Outcome
document_sections.content: Vitrectomy is often indicated when decreased acuity, metamorphopsia, diplopia, or difficulty using both eyes affects a patient with ERM or VMT. Table 2 presents study-specific surgical outcomes. Acuity improves by an average of 2 lines or more, but gains vary substantially, and 10% to 20% of patients have unchanged or worse vision. Mean NEI-VFQ-25 scores improved at both 6 and 24 months in a cited study. Metamorphopsia usually improves and may disappear; another study of 42 patients found improvements at 6 months in NEI-VFQ-25 scores, stereopsis, and distance BCVA. Relief of distortion may be valued even without acuity improvement. A study of 43 eyes associated intact preoperative inner photoreceptor and ellipsoid zone on OCT with better postoperative acuity. Another associated preserved ellipsoid zone and cone outer segment tips line with better acuity. Outer-retinal features may improve or normalize after surgery and correlate with improved acuity; a study of 101 eyes linked photoreceptor disruption to poorer postoperative vision. A systematic review and meta-analysis comparing combined with sequential pars plana vitrectomy and phacoemulsification for macular hole or ERM found no significant differences in complications or visual or refractive results.

document_sections.heading: Complications
document_sections.content: Most phakic patients develop progressive nuclear cataract after ERM vitrectomy. Retinal breaks and detachments appear less frequent with current techniques, possibly because of smaller instruments, cannulated incisions, improved peripheral visualization, and peripheral vitreous and break management. One 23-gauge series reported retinal breaks in approximately 1% of cases (8 of 548); another reported detachment in 1% (2 of 166). A study of 349 eyes reported detachment in 1% after 23-gauge versus 3.5% after 20-gauge vitrectomy. Reported endophthalmitis frequency is less than 0.05% of vitrectomies. Macular-hole formation after ERM or VMT surgery is another possible complication, with reported incidence of 2.1%.

document_sections.heading: Follow-up Evaluation after Surgery
document_sections.content: Patients should be assessed on postoperative day 1 and again at 1 to 2 weeks, or sooner if new symptoms or early findings warrant. High or low intraocular pressure, wound leakage, pain, worsening vision, or suspected retinal complications justify earlier or more frequent visits. Follow-up should cover interval symptoms, intraocular pressure, slit-lamp assessment of the anterior segment and wounds and, where possible, central retina, plus indirect binocular peripheral retinal examination. Patients should receive guidance about postoperative medications, retinal-detachment warning signs, and precautions if intraocular gas was used. Persistent diplopia or difficulty coordinating the eyes may warrant referral to a strabismus specialist or orthoptist.

document_sections.heading: PROVIDER AND SETTING
document_sections.content: Diagnosing and managing ERM, VMT, or VMA calls for specialized equipment, expertise, and, when needed, surgical skills. Referral to an ophthalmologist experienced with these conditions is recommended. Appropriately trained, supervised staff may perform diagnostic procedures, but interpretation and medical or surgical management require an ophthalmologist with vitreoretinal training and clinical and surgical judgment.

document_sections.heading: COUNSELING AND REFERRAL
document_sections.content: Patients should promptly report more floaters, loss of visual field, metamorphopsia, or decreased acuity to their ophthalmologist. Functionally limiting postoperative visual impairment warrants vision-rehabilitation and social-service referral. Empathic questioning can uncover concerns. Counseling, vocational rehabilitation, or peer support should be considered for depression, anxiety, or loss of independence or employment, particularly when a central or paracentral scotoma persists.

document_sections.heading: SOCIOECONOMIC CONSIDERATIONS
document_sections.content: A 2008 cost-utility analysis comparing ERM surgery with observation in the better-seeing eye estimated a mean gain of 0.755 discounted QALYs per treated patient at a 3% annual rate and a cost of $4,680 per QALY. Sensitivity analyses gave utility-related costs of $3,746 to $6,245/QALY gained and medical-cost results of $3,510 to $5,850/QALY gained. For surgery in the worse-seeing eye versus observation, estimated mean gain was 0.27 discounted QALYs per treated patient; cost was $16,146 per QALY, with a sensitivity-analysis range of $12,110 to $20,183. Utility-related values ranged from $12,916 to $21,520/QALY. The analysis characterized ERM surgery as highly cost-effective relative to other medical interventions.

document_sections.heading: APPENDIX 1. QUALITY OF OPHTHALMIC CARE CORE CRITERIA
document_sections.content: Quality eye care places the patient's interests first and combines clinical competence with compassion and respect for dignity. Ophthalmologists should maintain and assess their skills, respond to patients' needs, and secure appropriate care or referral when needed. Effective patient–physician communication includes explaining the condition, prognosis, options, and risks so patients can participate meaningfully in decisions. Clinical judgment should guide testing, treatment timing, and follow-up according to urgency and individual needs. Clinicians should perform procedures only within their competence or with qualified assistance; maintain continuity and suitable preoperative and postoperative arrangements; arrange alternate care when unavailable; and refer or consult according to patient needs and provider qualifications. They should keep accurate records, share them appropriately, review test and consultation results promptly, and identify themselves and their roles. When treatment fails and no further treatment is available, appropriate support, rehabilitation, social services, and referral remain important. Before invasive diagnostic or therapeutic procedures, clinicians should evaluate the patient sufficiently and explain the proposed intervention, alternatives, expected benefits and risks, chance of success, and implications of no treatment. New technology should be adopted judiciously in light of cost, comparative benefit, safety, and efficacy. Periodic review of personal performance, communication of unexpected complications to colleagues, appropriately equipped facilities, and cost-conscious care without unacceptable loss of quality are also core attributes.

document_sections.heading: APPENDIX 2. INTERNATIONAL STATISTICAL CLASSIFICATION OF DISEASES AND RELATED HEALTH PROBLEMS (ICD) CODES
document_sections.content: The appendix tabulates ICD-9 CM and ICD-10 CM codes for epiretinal membrane and vitreomacular traction or adhesion. For bilateral disease without a bilateral ICD-10 CM code, separate left- and right-side codes should be assigned; an unspecified code is reserved for situations without another code option. Where a diagnosis code expresses laterality, right corresponds to 1, left to 2, and bilateral to 3.

document_sections.heading: LITERATURE SEARCHES FOR THIS PPP
document_sections.content: PubMed was searched on March 6, 2023, with limited updates on January 23, 2024 and August 6, 2024. Filters targeted human, English-language randomized controlled trials and systematic reviews, with date limits for publications since June 1, 2019. Of 1,274 studies examined, 18 entered the guideline and 1,256 were excluded. Searches concerning patient values and preferences yielded 11 studies; searches concerning economic evaluation and treatment cost yielded 0 studies. The search topics also covered diagnosis, epidemiology, pathology, quality of life, risk factors, therapy, and costs.
